reasons: The mechanism is real and new to this programme. Liquidity provision after forced liquidation (Grossman-Miller, Nagel 2012) is a stated economic reason, not indicator soup. No prior test conditioned on volume. The v = 1.0 control arm and the monotone-in-v prediction make it falsifiable. It is not a duplicate of prior_cross_zfade or prior_index_meanrev under rule 8, provided the volume arms carry the result.

The registered thresholds give almost no trades. I counted only how often the conditions occur in 2010-2017, using 20:00-UTC-to-20:00-UTC days, ATR20 of prior true ranges and the 20-day volume ratio. I looked at no returns or outcomes. Shock days at k = 1.5 number 49-64 per market in design (about 2.5-3% of weekdays), not the 150-170 the rationale assumes (8% of days is roughly the k = 1.0 rate). With v = 1.75 only 2-8 shock days per market survive: EURUSD 2, GBPUSD 2, AUDUSD 2, USDJPY 6, AUDJPY 2, XAUUSD 8. With v = 2.5 there are 0-3. The registered minimum of 40 design trades per market cannot be met by any filtered arm, and the monotonicity kill rule would compare noise across arms of 0-8 trades.

The volume series is Dukascopy's summed bid-side quoted volume (edge/data/store.py: 'vol is bid-side tick volume'; values are quoted sizes, not traded volume). It responds only weakly to large days. In design the correlation of log(V/Vbar) with range/ATR is 0.22-0.42. The median ratio on k = 1.5 shock days is 1.15-1.26 against 1.00 on other days, and the 90th percentile on shock days is only 1.56-1.71. That is why v = 1.75 is so rare. The measure does flag known liquidation episodes and not scheduled data, which supports the mechanism. Ratios: SNB 2015-01-15 EURUSD 2.23; Brexit 2016-06-24 GBPUSD 2.41 and EURUSD 1.78; yen flash crash 2019-01-03 AUDJPY 1.79 and USDJPY 1.76; gold crash 2013-04-15 XAUUSD 2.95; NFP 2014-12-05 EURUSD 0.90; FOMC 2015-03-18 EURUSD 1.11. So the idea deserves a test with thresholds that fit how this series actually behaves.

Feasible thresholds come from the same frequency count, with no outcomes seen. Pooled over 6 markets in design: k = 1.0 gives 1048 shock days (v = 1.0), 336 (v = 1.3) and 150 (v = 1.5). k = 1.25 gives 585 / 218 / 95. Per market, k = 1.0 and v = 1.3 gives 42-67 trades, which matches the hypothesis's own target of 40-70.

Large FX days hit several markets at once. Brexit, SNB and the yen flash crash each show up in 3-5 of the six markets on the same date. Treating 6 markets x N days as independent overstates the pooled t. The kill rules lean on pooled evidence, so pooled statistics must be clustered by date.

The monotonicity kill rule as written cannot be met even if the effect is real. Per cell (one k, one hold, one market) the standard error of avg R at 20-60 trades is 0.08-0.15 R. A tolerance of 0.02 R across 8 step comparisons will fire by chance whatever the truth. The rule must be evaluated on pooled cells.

The prior is against plain reversal at this horizon. D1 AC1 is positive on EURUSD (+0.02), GBPUSD (+0.05), AUDUSD (+0.02) and XAUUSD (+0.03), and the related price-only fades are dead. Expect the v = 1.0 control to come out at or below zero. All of the edge has to come from the volume conditioning, and that is exactly what the kill rule tests. This is acceptable.
reviews.revisions: 1) Grid: k in [1.0, 1.25], v in [1.0, 1.3, 1.5], hold_days in [1, 3] (12 combinations). Defaults: k = 1.0, v = 1.3, sl_atr = 1.0, hold_days = 1. Record in the pre-registration that the thresholds were moved for sample-size feasibility from a frequency count with no outcomes examined, and that the original k = 1.5 / v = 1.75 / v = 2.5 arms were dropped because they hold 0-8 design trades per market. 2) Minimum trades: 40 per market in design at k = 1.0, v = 1.3, and 200 pooled. 3) Rewrite kill rule (2) on pooled stage-B design data (6 markets). For each v, compute avg R averaged over the four (k, hold) cells, with trades from all markets pooled. Require avg R(v = 1.5) >= avg R(v = 1.3) - 0.02, and max(avg R(1.3), avg R(1.5)) - avg R(1.0) >= 0.04. Then repeat the 0.04 gap test in the check period at the chosen (k, hold); failing it is a kill. 4) Pooled t-statistics in stage B, check and walk-forward are computed on date-clustered R: average the R of all markets that traded the same signal date into one observation, then compute t over dates. Report the unclustered figure alongside. 5) Exit timing: put the exit flag on the last bar before E(D + hold_days), not on E(D + hold_days). The trade then closes at the open of the bar that ends at 20:00 UTC on that date, and a new shock signal at E(D + hold_days) can register. With the rule as written, the executor sees the position still open when the next day's signal arrives and silently drops it. Shock days cluster, so that loses exactly the follow-on shocks. 6) Keep kill rules (1), (3) and (4) as written. Update expected numbers: per-market design t about 0.6-1.2 at 0.08 R, so stage A on EURUSD alone has a real chance of a false negative. The Director should know this before reading a stage A kill.
reviews.notes_for_builder: Volume: sum m.vol over H1 bars whose CLOSE time (ts + 1h, since bars are labelled by open time) lies in (20:00 UTC on D_prev, 20:00 UTC on D]. E(D) is the last bar whose close time is in (16:00, 20:00] UTC on D, so normally the bar opening 19:00. Vbar(D) is the mean of the previous 20 valid V values, strictly before D (no D in its own mean). Use a loop over dates, not bars. Skip if Vbar <= 0 or V is not finite. ret(D) uses bid_c at E(D) and E(D_prev), with D - D_prev <= 4 calendar days. ATR: daily.to_bars(F.atr_prev(daily, 20)) read at index E(D); E(D) at 19:00-20:00 UTC lies inside the NY trading day that started the previous evening, so atr_prev is already shifted. Signal on bar E(D): entry_long if ret < 0, entry_short if ret > 0, entry_type 0, valid_bars 1, sl_dist = sl_atr * ATR, tp NaN, max_bars = 24 * (hold_days + 3). Exit flag goes on index X - 1, where X = E of the hold_days-th later valid date (the oracle pattern exit_long[xi - 1]), and only if X - 1 > E(D). Monday windows include Friday-evening and Sunday-open hours. Accept this as specified; do not renormalise. XAUUSD has artefact minutes holding up to 91% of a day's volume. Do not filter them (no new knobs), but list the dates of the XAUUSD climax trades in the stage C report so artefact-driven signals can be seen. Weekday of D must be Mon-Fri. No other filters.

reasons: This is not a duplicate of prior_flow_atlas. I checked run_flow_atlas.py: its 18 day types are weekdays, gotobi, month-start and month-end ordinals, and US, Japan and England holidays. There is no calendar-month condition, and its windows are at most 8 hours, so a two-month seasonal was outside its search space. The atlas's Bonferroni bar (t >= 3.7) covers re-slices of that space, not a single pre-registered replication of a published anomaly. prior_trend_follow and prior_index_meanrev did not condition on month either.

The primary arm does not match the published claim. The rationale cites Baur (2013) for positive returns concentrated in September and November, yet the primary window is sep_oct, which includes October and drops November. A confirmatory test must test what was published (September and November), or the replication is itself a choice made after the fact.

mar_apr is not a clean control. Indian physical demand has a second peak around Akshaya Tritiya (April-May) and the spring wedding season, so March-April is not a no-demand season under the hypothesis's own mechanism. Kill rule (2) is meant to separate seasonal demand from gold's general drift in the same years. The right comparison is every other month of the same years (the rest of the year, Mon-Thu, same 24-hour structure).

Executor mismatch that silently halves and biases the sample. The rules exit on E(D_next), so the position closes at the open of the bar after E(D_next). At the close of E(D_next) the position is still open, and the executor ignores entries while a position is open (executor.py: 'register this bar's signals (ignored while a position is open)'). Every second day is therefore skipped, and the trades fall on Mondays and Wednesdays only. The sample halves to about 150 design trades and a day-of-week pattern enters that the hypothesis never registered. The text accepts 'the day is skipped', but here it is systematic, not occasional.

Power and usefulness. By its own numbers (+0.02 to +0.04 R per trade, per-trade sd about 0.4 R at a 2 x ATR stop, about 280 trades), design t is about 1.0-1.7. It can reach the programme's t >= 2 bar only if the effect is larger than the literature suggests. Even if real, Sep + Nov at about 35 trades a year x 0.03 R is about 1 R a year, a minor contributor to a +10% phase. It is cheap and a clean out-of-sample reading of a published anomaly, so it is worth a small amount of compute. The Director should expect an honest negative or a sub-bar positive.

Long-only on gold carries luck risk. Long-only tests on rising assets pass the bar 2-8% of the time. 2024-2026 is a strong gold bull market, so a positive holdout from a long-only gold rule is weak evidence by itself. The seasonal claim must be judged as the window minus the control, in check and in the holdout, not as raw avg R.

Costs are negligible. Spread plus slippage of about 34 pips against a 2 x ATR20 stop of about 4500 pips is under 0.01 R. One night of financing at policy rate + 1% on a 2-3% stop distance is about 0.003 R.
reviews.revisions: 1) Windows: "sep_nov_baur" = D in September or November (the published months; primary), "sep_nov" = September 1 to November 30 (the broader physical-demand season), "rest" = every other month (January-August and December; the control). Drop sep_oct and mar_apr. Grid: window x sl_atr [1.0, 2.0] = 6 combinations. Default window = sep_nov_baur, sl_atr = 2.0. 2) Kill rule (1) moves to sep_nov_baur at sl_atr = 2.0. Kill rule (2) becomes: in design, avg R(sep_nov_baur) - avg R(rest) >= 0.02 at the same stop, otherwise kill regardless of sign. Kill rule (4) adds: in check, avg R(window) - avg R(rest) > 0 at the chosen combination. If promoted, the holdout verdict must also report the window-minus-rest difference, and a holdout where the window does not beat the rest is a fail even if raw avg R > 0. Pre-register this now. 3) Kill rule (3), seasons not days: at least 5 of 8 design seasons (Sep + Nov R sum per year) positive. Keep it. 4) Exit: set exit_long on the last bar before E(D_next), not on E(D_next). The trade then closes at the open of the bar ending at 20:00 UTC on D_next (about a 23-hour hold), the position is flat when the next day's signal registers at E(D_next), and every Mon-Thu day in the window trades. Minimum design trades: 250 for sep_nov_baur. 5) Update expectations: design t 1.0-1.7 is accepted as below the pass bar. Register that a pass needs design t >= 2, which this test reaches only if the effect is stronger than published.
reviews.notes_for_builder: H1 bars are labelled by open time. E(D) is the last bar on UTC date D whose close (ts + 1h) is in (16:00, 20:00] UTC, normally the bar opening 19:00. Window membership uses the UTC month of D. window is a string param read from p['window'], with values sep_nov_baur (months 9 and 11), sep_nov (months 9-11) and rest (months 1-8 and 12); raise on any other value. Weekday of D must be Mon-Thu. ATR: daily.to_bars(F.atr_prev(daily, 20))[E(D)]; skip if NaN or <= 0. Entry: entry_long[E(D)] = True, type 0, valid_bars 1, sl_dist = sl_atr * ATR, tp NaN, max_bars = 30. Exit: let X = E(D_next), where D_next is the next UTC date with a valid E (any weekday, including Friday). Set exit_long[X - 1] = True only if X - 1 > E(D) (oracle pattern exit_long[xi - 1]). Do not add an entry on Fridays or weekends. Loop over dates, not bars. No other filters.
